deep.summary: The quote originates anonymously in a 12-step recovery community (earliest documented form: Knoxville News-Sentinel, October 11, 1981, quoting an unnamed Al-Anon member), was refined in an NA approval draft the same month, popularized in Rita Mae Brown's 1983 novel Sudden Death, and was not attributed to Einstein until 1990—the attribution is a confirmed fabrication listed under 'Misattributed to Einstein' in Princeton University Press's authoritative The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

origin.title: Al-Anon Helps Family, Friends to Orderly Lives (Knoxville News-Sentinel)

changes: Attribution fabricated: the quote originated anonymously in a 12-step recovery community (Al-Anon meeting, Oct 1981); Einstein's name was not attached until 1990, 35 years after his death, with no primary source ever produced.
Wording drift from NA (1981): 'repeating the same mistakes' became 'doing the same thing' in Brown's 1983 novel and in the most widely circulated version.
Conjunction change: Brown's 1983 novel uses 'but expecting different results'; the circulated claim uses 'and expecting different results'.
Addition of 'The definition of insanity is…' framing: neither the 1981 nor the 1983 sources use the definite-article 'definition' construction; this was added by later users.
'A different result' (singular, 1990 Earle attribution) became 'different results' (plural) in later popular versions.

steps.exact_wording: Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.

steps.exact_wording: Insanity is repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results.

steps.title: Sudden Death — Rita Mae Brown (Bantam Books, New York)

steps.note: Uses 'but expecting' not 'and expecting'; attributed within the novel to a fictional character (Jane Fulton), not to Einstein. First wide-print appearance of the 'doing the same thing' phrasing. Brown likely recycled a phrase already circulating in recovery communities.

deep.summary: The '10% of the brain' claim has no identifiable primary scientific source; it evolved from William James's 1907 metaphor about untapped mental energy (no percentage, no brain reference) through a 1929 anonymous self-help advertisement and Lowell Thomas's uncited 1936 attribution to James, with each retelling adding precision and neurological specificity the original never contained, until the vague philosophical observation became a blunt and false neuroscientific assertion.
changes: James (1907) used 'small part of our possible mental and physical resources' — no percentage, no brain reference, concept is energy/potential not neurology
1929 World Almanac ad added the explicit '10 percent' figure and shifted the subject to 'brain power', but was anonymous advertising copy with no scientific backing

Lowell Thomas (1936) attached '10 percent' to William James by name without any citation, changed 'resources' to 'latent mental ability', and framed it as a reported recollection ('used to say') rather than a quotation
Self-help writers (e.g., Witt, 1983) further shifted 'latent mental ability' to 'brainpower', implying a neurological claim about the brain organ
Popular culture (advertising, films such as Lucy 2014) converted the claim into an explicit, blunt neurological assertion: 'uses 10% of their brain capacity', presented as scientific fact
Albert Einstein was falsely inserted as an authority for the claim; the Einstein Archives found no such statement
No peer-reviewed study, clinical report, or official dataset has ever been found making the '10% of the brain' claim as a measured scientific finding

steps.title: The Energies of Men (William James, 1907)
steps.exact_wording: We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.
steps.note: No percentage stated; refers to mental and physical resources/energy, not the brain as an organ; claim about untapped potential, not neurology

steps.title: World Almanac self-help advertisement (reproduced in Mind Myths, 1999)
steps.exact_wording: There is NO LIMIT to what the human brain can accomplish. Scientists and psychologists tell us we use only about TEN PERCENT of our brain power.
steps.note: First known explicit '10 percent of brain power' statement; anonymous advertising copy, not a scientific source; no specific scientist cited; known only via secondary reproduction in Mind Myths (1999)

steps.title: Introduction: A Shortcut to Distinction (Lowell Thomas foreword to Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People)
steps.exact_wording: Professor William James of Harvard used to say that the average man develops only ten percent of his latent mental ability.
steps.note: Second-hand attribution ('used to say'), no citation to any James text; narrows James's 'mental and physical resources' to 'latent mental ability'; attaches precise 10% figure James never used; still refers to mental ability, not brain tissue

steps.title: How to Be Twice as Smart (Scott Witt, 1983)
steps.exact_wording: If you're like most people, you're using only ten percent of your brainpower.
steps.note: Shifts from 'latent mental ability' to 'brainpower', implying the brain organ; no scientific source cited; self-help book, Prentice Hall

steps.title: The Ten-Percent Myth (Benjamin Radford, Skeptical Inquirer, March/April 1999)
steps.exact_wording: The origins of the myth are not at all clear. Beyerstein, of the Brain Behaviour Laboratory at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, has traced it back to at least the early part of the century.
steps.note: Debunking article; confirms no clear origin found; refers readers to Beyerstein's Mind Myths chapter for detailed analysis; does not itself resolve the origin

steps.title: Great myths of the brain: We only use 10 per cent (Christian Jarrett, BPS Psychologist, summarising Beyerstein's Mind Myths chapter)
steps.exact_wording: The journalist Lowell Thomas aided this process in his preface to Dale Carnegie's mega-selling 1936 self-help book How to Win Friends and Influence People, where he attached the precise 10 percent figure to James's point about potential, writing: "Professor William James of Harvard used to say that the average person develops only 10 percent of his latent mental ability."
steps.note: Secondary summary of Beyerstein's findings; confirms Thomas as the vector who added the precise percentage to James's vaguer claim; notes James 'didn't put a precise figure on it'

deep.summary: The claim originates as speculative rhetorical hyperbole in a 1754 letter by William Stukeley (published 1887), was amplified by Henry Norman (1895) and Ripley's Believe It or Not! (1932), given false scientific authority by Richard Halliburton (1938), and is comprehensively refuted by NASA and astronaut testimony—the wall is not visible from the Moon and only marginally detectable from low Earth orbit under exceptional conditions with optical aids.

origin.title: The Family Memoirs of the Rev. William Stukeley (letter of 1754, published 1887, Surtees Society, Vol. 3, p. 142)
origin.exact_wording: This mighty wall [Hadrian's Wall] of four score miles [130 km] in length is only exceeded by the Chinese Wall, which makes a considerable figure upon the terrestrial globe, and may be discerned at the Moon.

changes: Stukeley (1754): speculative hedge ('may be discerned') about Hadrian's Wall with Chinese Wall mentioned comparatively; not a direct claim about China's wall
Norman (1895): converted to reported reputation ('enjoys the reputation'); now explicitly about China's wall as 'the only work of human hands' visible from moon
Ripley (1932): all hedging removed; presented as confident mass-audience assertion; added 'mightiest work of man' superlative
Halliburton (1938): fabricated scientific authority by attributing claim to 'astronomers'; entered textbooks as pseudo-scientific consensus
Modern popular form: 'Moon' replaced by 'space'; 'only man-made' qualifier dropped; claim generalized and all original caveats removed

steps.title: The Family Memoirs of the Rev. William Stukeley (letter of 1754, published 1887, Surtees Society, Vol. 3, p. 142)
steps.exact_wording: This mighty wall [Hadrian's Wall] of four score miles [130 km] in length is only exceeded by the Chinese Wall, which makes a considerable figure upon the terrestrial globe, and may be discerned at the Moon.
steps.note: Origin: speculative comparative aside about Hadrian's Wall; Chinese Wall mentioned parenthetically; hedged with 'may be discerned'; not a claim about China's wall specifically

steps.title: The Peoples and Politics of the Far East, Henry Norman, p. 215
steps.exact_wording: Besides its age it enjoys the reputation of being the only work of human hands on the globe visible from the moon.
steps.note: Converts Stukeley's speculative 'may be discerned' into a reported social reputation; adds 'only work of human hands'; no longer hedged as speculation but framed as established lore

steps.title: Ripley's Believe It or Not! newspaper cartoon
steps.exact_wording: the mightiest work of man, the only one that would be visible to the human eye from the moon.
steps.note: Removes all hedging; presented as confident assertion to mass readership; adds superlative 'mightiest work of man'; speculation fully dropped

steps.title: Second Book of Marvels – The Orient, Richard Halliburton (Bobbs-Merrill, 1938)

steps.note: Fabricates scientific authority by attributing claim to 'astronomers'; no astronomer ever made this claim; enters popular and textbook culture as pseudo-scientific fact

steps.title: Great Wall – NASA (PDF: great_wall_less_great_from_space.pdf)
steps.exact_wording: It has become a space-based myth. The Great Wall of China, frequently billed as the only man-made object visible from space, generally isn't, at least to the unaided eye in low Earth orbit. It certainly isn't visible from the Moon.
steps.note: Official NASA refutation; traces myth only to 1938 (Halliburton), omitting Stukeley 1754 and Norman 1895; confirms the claim is false

deep.summary: No primary source for the 'eight spiders a year' claim has ever been found; the most widely cited origin story (a 1993 article by 'Lisa Birgit Holst' in 'PC Professional') was a deliberate April 2001 hoax by Snopes, admitted in August 2021, and the actual origin of this urban legend — which exists in multiple incompatible numerical versions — remains unknown.
changes: The number of spiders shifts freely across sources: 'eight per year,' 'four per year,' 'twenty in a lifetime,' 'eight in a lifetime,' and 'a pound in a lifetime' — no stable figure exists, indicating the statistic was never measured.
Snopes's 2001 article introduced a completely fabricated origin story (Holst / PC Professional / 1954 book / page 24) that was treated as fact by thousands of secondary sources for two decades.
The 1954 book 'Insect Fact and Folklore' is real but does not contain the spider-swallowing claim; Snopes's own follow-up page confirmed this.
The 1999 trivia listicle used 'eight in a lifetime,' but most later popular sources shifted to 'eight per year' — a significant escalation with no basis.
The Burke Museum's authoritative page uses 'four' per year, not 'eight' — the expert debunker's version of the claim itself differs from the most common popular form.
Some sources mistakenly attribute the Chicago Sun-Times article to 'Ellen Domke' and others to 'Zay N. Smith,' showing secondary-source copying errors in even the bibliographic record.
The Snapple cap version elevated an urban legend to a branded consumer 'Real Fact,' giving the unverified claim a commercial imprimatur.

steps.exact_wording: The average person swallows eight spiders a year while sleeping. What if all eight show up tonight?
steps.note: Reported by one secondary blog source as the earliest known print appearance; tongue-in-cheek in context; not independently confirmed in available primary evidence. If real, it predates all other references but was not asserting the claim as fact.

Smith, not Ellen Domke — author attribution is inconsistent across sources. Treated the claim as received trivia, not as an original assertion.

steps.title: '50 Top Pieces of Trivia' listicle (source: Snopes citation)

steps.note: Quoted verbatim by Snopes's Lisa Birgit Holst page as evidence the legend predated Snopes. Notably says 'lifetime' not 'per year' — a significant variation from the most common form of the claim.

steps.title: Snopes.com: 'Do People Swallow Eight Spiders Per Year?' (original article, fabricated citation)
steps.exact_wording: This 'statistic' average the average person swallowing eight spiders per year was not only made up out of whole cloth, it was invented as an example of the absurd things people will believe simply because they come across them on the Internet.
steps.note: Attributed the claim's origin to a nonexistent journalist ('Lisa Birgit Holst'), a nonexistent magazine ('PC Professional'), and a nonexistent passage in a real 1954 book. changes: The original 1965 source was a commercial product slogan ('Healthcare with 10,000 steps/day'), not a scientific prescription; no 'you need' framing existed.

Hatano's 1960s caloric arithmetic was a theoretical estimate (300 kcal/day), not a clinical trial or validated health threshold; it was later cited academically but never constituted a formal guideline.

Tudor-Locke & Bassett 2004 introduced 10,000 steps as the lower boundary of their 'active' pedometer classification index, a preliminary research heuristic that was widely misread as a health recommendation.
The 2008 Tudor-Locke/Hatano paper explicitly stated 10,000 steps is 'commonly promoted despite any authoritative endorsement,' but popular media ignored this caveat.
The word 'need' (implying necessity and a minimum threshold) was added by popular media and fitness-tracker defaults, with no basis in the original slogan or any scientific source.
The Lee 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine study found mortality benefits plateau at ~7,500 steps/day in older women, directly contradicting the 10,000-step necessity claim.
Fitbit and other wearables setting 10,000 as the default goal laundered the marketing origin into an apparent technical/health standard, reinforcing the misquoted claim.

steps.title: YAMAX | Pedometer | About us — Yamasa Tokei Keiki Co., Ltd.
steps.exact_wording: Developed and launched the first pedometer 'Manpo Meter' under the slogan of 'Healthcare with 10,000 steps/day'. The well-known among world by word for pedometer 'Manpo-kei' (Manpo means 10,000 steps in Japanese) is our trademark.
steps.note: Primary origin: a commercial product slogan, not a scientific finding. No study cited. No necessity ('you need') implied.

steps.title: Hatano Y. Use of the pedometer for promoting daily walking exercise. ICHPER-SD Journal 29:4–8.
steps.exact_wording: Dr. Yoshiro Hatano correlated 10,000 steps with approximately 300 kcal expended, which encourages adherence to healthful physical activity levels. [Cited in Tudor-Locke et al. 2008 and PMC9022022]
steps.note: Earliest identifiable academic publication linking 10,000 steps to a health rationale (caloric expenditure estimate). Not a clinical trial. Not directly accessible in evidence set; known only through secondary citations.

steps.title: Tudor-Locke C, Bassett DR Jr. How Many Steps/Day Are Enough? Sports Medicine 34(1):1–8.
steps.exact_wording: A value of 10 000 steps/day is gaining popularity with the media and in practice and can be traced to Japanese walking clubs and a business slogan 30+ years ago.
steps.note: First major academic paper to trace the origin to Japanese walking clubs and a business slogan. Explicitly not an authoritative endorsement. Introduces preliminary pedometer indices, labeling ≥10,000 steps/day as 'active'—this classification was later misread as a health prescription.

steps.title: Tudor-Locke C, Hatano Y, Pangrazi RP, Kang M. Revisiting 'How Many Steps Are Enough?' Med. Sci. Sports Exerc. 40(7S):S537–S543.
steps.exact_wording: This increasingly popular index can be traced to the 1960s when Japanese walking clubs embraced a pedometer manufacturer's (Yamasa Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) nickname for their product: manpo-kei (literally translated, 'ten thousand steps meter'). A value of 10,000 steps/day is often associated with a healthful level of PA ... and is commonly promoted despite any authoritative endorsement.
steps.note: Confirms origin in marketing/walking clubs with no authoritative health endorsement. The phrase 'despite any authoritative endorsement' directly contradicts the popular claim's implied authority.

steps.title: Lee IM et al. Association of Step Volume and Intensity With All-Cause Mortality in Older Women. JAMA Internal Medicine 179(8):1105–1112.
steps.exact_wording: A goal of 10 000 steps/d is commonly believed by the public to be necessary for health, but this number has limited scientific basis. However, the origin of the goal of 10 000 steps per day is unclear. It likely derives from the trade name of a pedometer sold in 1965 by Yamasa Clock and Instrument Company in Japan called Manpo-kei, which translates to '10 000 steps meter' in Japanese.
steps.note: Landmark peer-reviewed study. Explicitly states the 10,000-step goal has 'limited scientific basis.' Finds mortality benefit plateaus at ~7,500 steps/day in older women, well below 10,000.

steps.title: 10,000 steps a day — or fewer? Harvard Health Publishing
steps.exact_wording: Dr. Lee discovered that the origins of the number go back to 1965, when a Japanese company made a device named Manpo-kei, which translates to '10,000 steps meter.' 'The name was a marketing tool,' she says.
steps.note: High-credibility secondary summary. Correctly attributes origin to marketing tool. Transmits the nuance of the Lee 2019 findings accurately but adds lay-accessible framing.

trail.title: Marie Antoinette: “Qu’ils mangent de la brioche"
trail.wording: 12016-06-23T01:04:26-07:00Gary Walker-Robertsff82d71fc8661901c549a69ff80c9bac7b614722100945image\header2016-06-24T07:50:41-07:00Gary Walker-Robertsff82d71fc8661901c549a69ff80c9bac7b614722 “Qu’ils mang

deep.summary: The quote originates in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Confessions (c.1765–1767), where an unnamed 'great princess' says 'let them eat brioche'; it was never attributed to Marie Antoinette in any contemporary source, the first hedged printed link to her name appeared in Alphonse Karr's Les Guêpes in 1841 (48 years after her death), and the popular English form 'Let them eat cake — Marie Antoinette' compounds a chronological impossibility with a mistranslation.

origin.title: Les Confessions, Livre VI
origin.exact_wording: Enfin je me rappelai le pis-aller d'une grande princesse à qui l'on disait que les paysans n'avaient pas de pain, et qui répondit : Qu'ils mangent de la brioche.

changes: Speaker changed: Rousseau's unnamed 'une grande princesse' became 'Marie Antoinette' — first tentatively in Karr 1841, then in popular discourse, with no evidentiary basis.
Food changed: 'brioche' (rich buttery bread) mistranslated as 'cake' in popular English renderings; one 1901 translation used 'pastry' instead.
Certainty inflated: Karr introduced the name with explicit doubt ('vrai ou faux'); popular usage dropped all hedging and stated the attribution as fact.
Context stripped: the original is a passing recalled anecdote in Rousseau's autobiography about his own hunger; popular usage frames it as a defiant royal declaration to starving subjects.
Timeline ignored: Rousseau wrote the passage c.1765–1767 when Marie Antoinette was approximately 9–11 years old and living in Vienna, making attribution to her chronologically impossible.

steps.title: Les Confessions, Livre VI — Jean-Jacques Rousseau
steps.exact_wording: Enfin je me rappelai le pis-aller d'une grande princesse à qui l'on disait que les paysans n'avaient pas de pain, et qui répondit : Qu'ils mangent de la brioche.
steps.note: Origin. Speaker is unnamed ('une grande princesse'); food is brioche, not cake; published posthumously 1782; Marie Antoinette was ~9–11 years old in Vienna when written.

steps.title: Les Guêpes — Alphonse Karr, November 1841
steps.exact_wording: Cet aperçu rappelle le mot vrai ou faux qu'on rapporte de Marie Antoinette
steps.note: First known printed link of Marie Antoinette's name to the saying, but explicitly hedged as 'true or false' (vrai ou faux); Karr is reporting a rumour, not asserting fact.

steps.title: Les Guêpes — Alphonse Karr, April 1843
steps.exact_wording: Le hasard m'a fait un de ces jours derniers rencontrer un livre daté de 1760 — où on raconte le même mot d'une duchesse de Toscane, — ce qui me paraît prouver à peu près que le mot n'a pas été dit par Marie-Antoinette, mais retrouvé et mis en circulation contre elle.
steps.note: Karr cites a 1760 book attributing the phrase to a Duchess of Tuscany and explicitly argues Marie Antoinette did NOT say it; paradoxically, naming her to refute the claim cemented the association in public discourse.

steps.title: Campion-Vincent & Shojaei Kawan, 'Marie-Antoinette et son célèbre dire', Annales historiques de la Révolution française
steps.exact_wording: MARIE-ANTOINETTE ET SON CÉLÈBRE DIRE : DEUX SCÉNOGRAPHIES ET DEUX SIÈCLES DE DÉSORDRES, TROIS NIVEAUX DE COMMUNICATION ET TROIS MODES ACCUSATOIRES
steps.note: Scholarly study confirming Karr 1841 is earliest located written link between Marie Antoinette and the phrase; found no attribution in revolutionary-era press, pamphlets, caricatures, or trial records.

steps.title: Popular English-language diffusion: 'Let them eat cake — Marie Antoinette'
steps.exact_wording: Let them eat cake. — Marie Antoinette
steps.note: Modern popular form. Introduces two errors absent from every earlier source: (1) replaces unnamed 'grande princesse' with 'Marie Antoinette'; (2) mistranslates 'brioche' as 'cake'. No primary source supports this wording or attribution.

origin.title: News: Does sugar make kids hyper? That's... (CNN News) - Behind the headlines - NLM

trail.title: News: Does sugar make kids hyper? That's... (CNN News) - Behind the headlines - NLM
trail.wording: Many parents blame sugar for their children’s hyperactive behavior.

trail.title: Is sugar making my child hyper? | News
trail.wording: Sugar itself may not make your child hyper, but it does affect your child’s health and future.

trail.title: Were your kids on a sugar high last night? Experts say it’s all in your head
trail.wording: The science shows pretty conclusively that sugar itself doesn’t make children hyperactive.

trail.title: Does sugar make kids hyper? What the research says (for teachers)
trail.wording: The claim: “Sugar makes children hyperactive.”

deep.summary: The claim 'sugar makes children hyperactive' has no primary scientific source asserting it as a finding; it is a folk extrapolation from Feingold's 1975 book about food additives (which did not implicate sugar), and every controlled primary study in the citation trail — including the definitive Wolraich et al. 1995 JAMA meta-analysis — directly refutes it.
changes: Feingold (1975) claimed food additives — not sugar — cause hyperactivity; sugar was absent from his original diet; the public conflated the two
The 1978 hypoglycemia study found a metabolic correlate; popular press interpreted this as sugar causing hyperactivity, which the study did not assert
Milich & Pelham (1986) and Rosen et al. (1988) found null or clinically insignificant effects; these refutations were largely ignored in popular discourse
Hoover & Milich (1994) showed parental expectation — not sugar — drives perceived hyperactivity; popular media sometimes cited this as confirmation that parents 'observe' sugar effects
Wolraich et al. (1995) JAMA meta-analysis concluded sugar does not affect behavior or cognition; popular claim strips all caveats and reverses the actual finding

The popular claim 'sugar makes children hyperactive' is a folk extrapolation from Feingold's additive theory, amplified by media, with no primary scientific source that asserts it as a supported finding

steps.title: Medical literature, 1922 (unnamed source)
steps.exact_wording: The notion that sugar might make children behave badly first appeared in the medical literature in 1922.
steps.note: Reported only by NYT (2020) as a secondary attribution; original 1922 document, author, and journal are unidentified and unverifiable from available evidence

steps.title: Why Your Child Is Hyperactive — Benjamin F. Feingold, Random House
steps.exact_wording: Feingold (1975) claimed that food additives cause hyperactivity in children. [Book promoted] a diet for children (and families) that eliminated food additives and colorings.
steps.note: Feingold's claim was about food additives, colorings, and salicylates — not sugar. Sugar was not mentioned in the original diet. The public conflated sugar-rich foods with additive-rich foods, producing the sugar-hyperactivity myth as a folk extrapolation.

steps.title: 1978 study on reactive hypoglycemia in hyperactive children — Food and Cosmetics Toxicology
steps.exact_wording: hyperactive children given glucose tolerance tests had results that suggested reactive hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). As yet, though, there are no good theories to explain the connection.
steps.note: First empirical bridge connecting sugar metabolism to hyperactivity-related phenomena; did not assert sugar causes hyperactivity; interpreted in popular press as supporting the causal claim

steps.title: Effects of sugar ingestion on the classroom and playground behavior of attention deficit disordered boys — Milich & Pelham (1986)
steps.exact_wording: Results offer no support for the contention that sugar ingestion adversely affects the behavior or learning of ADD boys.
steps.note: One of several pre-1990 controlled studies finding null results; directly contradicts the popular claim; belief attributed to children's difficulty readjusting after snack periods

steps.title: Effects of sugar ingestion expectancies on mother-child interactions — Hoover & Milich, Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology 22(4)
steps.exact_wording: This study tested the hypothesis that commonly reported negative effects of sugar on children's behavior may be due to parental expectancies. A challenge study design was employed, in which thirty-five 5- to 7-year-old boys reported by their mothers to be behaviorally 'sugar sensitive,' and their mothers, were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups... all children actually received the placebo (aspartame). Mothers in the sugar expectancy condition rated their children as significantly more hyperactive.
steps.note: Refutes the claim by showing the perceived effect is entirely driven by parental expectation; all children received placebo; frequently cited by popular media as contextualizing the myth without distorting its conclusion

steps.title: The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children: A meta-analysis — Wolraich, Wilson & White, JAMA 274(20)
steps.exact_wording: The meta-analytic synthesis of the studies to date found that sugar does not affect the behavior or cognitive performance of children. The strong belief of parents may be due to expectancy and common association. However, a small effect of sugar or effects on subsets of children cannot be ruled out.
steps.note: Definitive scientific refutation of the claim; 16 reports, 23 within-subject blinded studies, all 95% CIs include zero; frequently correctly summarized in secondary sources but stands in direct opposition to the popular claim
